analysis.investment_thesis: India Shelter is a textbook Lynch fast grower — 44% net profit CAGR at just 18.4x earnings yields a PEG of 0.41, one of the most compelling growth-at-a-price setups I've seen in Indian financials. The "Housing for All" story is visible from the street: millions of underserved tier 2/3 city borrowers need affordable home loans, and this company is positioned squarely in that white space.
key_strengths: PEG ratio of 0.41 (P/E 18.4x ÷ 44.4% profit CAGR) — exceptional value for a proven fast grower
Conservative leverage at D/E 1.88x vs. HFC peers at 4-6x, leaving massive headroom to scale the loan book
Accelerating profitability: EBITDA growing at 47.5% CAGR, faster than revenue (38.5%), signaling operating leverage
key_risks: Credit quality risk — small-ticket loans to informal-economy borrowers in semi-urban India are inherently higher NPA-prone
Finance cost growing at 35.4% CAGR (INR 106→356 Cr); any adverse rate cycle could compress net interest margins
Competitive squeeze from large banks and established HFCs (HDFC, Bajaj Housing) moving down-market into affordable segment
red_flags: Other income collapsed from INR 32 Cr (FY24) to INR 10 Cr (FY25) — suggests one-time income reversal that inflated prior earnings; quality of earnings needs scrutiny

Negative OCF every single year (-INR 1,435 Cr in FY25) — structurally normal for lending businesses (loan disbursements = outflows), but scale of cash consumption requires uninterrupted capital market access
analysis.detailed_analysis:
India Shelter is exactly the kind of stock I used to hunt for at Fidelity — a small, focused company in a giant market that Wall Street (or Dalal Street) hasn't fully priced in. The numbers are hard to argue with: revenue has compounded at 38.5% over four years from INR 317 Cr to INR 1,166 Cr, and net profit has grown even faster at 44.4% CAGR, from INR 87 Cr to INR 378 Cr. At 18.4x earnings on 44% growth, the PEG of 0.41 is well under my preferred threshold of 1.0 — in fact it's closer to the "back up the truck" territory. The forward P/E of 14.34x makes this even more attractive if growth sustains even at half its historical rate.

The negative operating cash flow looks alarming but is the single biggest misread on this stock. For a housing finance company, loan disbursements hit the operating cash flow statement — it's like penalizing a retailer for buying inventory. The real story is the financing CF of INR 1,566 Cr in FY25 funding a loan book that grew total assets from INR 2,463 Cr to INR 8,580 Cr in four years. What I genuinely like is the capital discipline: D/E of 1.88x is a fraction of what peers carry, meaning management isn't chasing growth recklessly. ROE of 15.1% is respectable but should expand as leverage is judiciously increased. The risk I'd watch most closely is asset quality — if the NPA cycle turns in affordable housing, this stock reprices fast. But at a PEG of 0.41, you're getting well compensated for that risk.
